features.description: NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeatedly compare pointer values with `cmp`, branch on equality with `jz`, then on the non-equal path form an offset address with `lea rsi [rax+CONST]` and pass it to a helper with `call`.
Incoming SysV argument values are copied from `rdi`/`rsi`/`rdx`/`r8` into callee-saved registers or stack slots so they can be reused across subsequent calls.
The code repeatedly decodes low-bit and byte fields by masking or shifting integers, testing the resulting values with `test` or `cmp`, and materializing boolean predicates with `setz` or `movzx`.

Repeated `push` instructions load stack-slot values, registers, addresses, and constants as stack-passed arguments immediately before a call with more arguments than fit in the six SysV integer argument registers.
Repeated internal `endbr64`-prefixed branch stubs jump to a `JUMP_ADDR_n`, often after moving `rax` into a callee-saved register.

A table-driven byte-processing pattern repeatedly masks or shifts values into indices, loads zero-extended entries with `movzx` from a base-plus-index address, and combines the results with integer arithmetic.
Many functions preserve an integer return status in `r12d` and copy it to `eax` immediately before restoring saved registers and returning.
The feature is integer bounds checking: a `cmp`/`test` of an index or count against a limit followed by a conditional jump such as `jbe`, `ja`, `jl`, or `js`, often to control loop termination.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN

A recurring range-dispatch idiom compares the same integer with immediate bounds in consecutive `cmp` instructions, branches first on a strict-above condition (`jg`/`ja`) and then on an inclusive-at-least condition (`jge`/`jnb`), and routes the remaining path with an unconditional `jmp`.
A lock-prefixed atomic operation appears as a normalized `lock ...` instruction, often near a conditional branch guarding the operation.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated indexed-byte loops compare zero-extended bytes with `cmp`, use unsigned `cmova` to select the smaller byte, then store the selected low byte back to an array.

Repeated object-dispatch-table checks load an object’s pointer, compare it with a global or code address, then compare a slot at a constant offset with an immediate-derived value and branch based on the result.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A recurring byte-field validation idiom applies `test` with an immediate bit mask to the low 8-bit subregister of a freshly loaded or computed scalar, then branches on the resulting flags.
The code repeatedly follows object pointers through fields, increments or decrements in-memory reference counts with `add`/`sub [register+offset], CONST`, and branches on zero to cleanup paths.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A stack-based temporary buffer is zeroed with `pxor xmm0,xmm0` and `movaps [rsp+...],xmm0`, then its address is passed in `rsi` to a helper call.
The code repeatedly extracts and updates packed bitfields by shifting 32-bit register values, masking them with `and`, combining them with `or`, and storing the result.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A range-checked switch dispatch loads a sign-extended offset from an indexed jump table, adds the table base, and jumps indirectly through the resulting register.

A pointer-linked ordered-tree traversal repeatedly loads node fields at fixed offsets, compares a key, and uses the comparison result to select the next node with conditional branches and `cmovcc`/`setcc`.
Repeated bitfield packing: load byte or word fragments from indexed memory, mask and shift them by a count in `CL`, OR the fragments together, and store the assembled value.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
The code repeatedly tests values and uses conditional jumps such as `jz`, `jnz`, and `js` to intra-function `JUMP_ADDR` blocks, with `jmp JUMP_ADDR` instructions linking basic blocks.
Repeated bit-field manipulation using shifts or rotates and masks, then combining the resulting pieces with bitwise `or` and `xor`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated SIMD computation in which XMM/YMM arithmetic results feed into further vector operations, often with unpacking, packing, or shuffling.
SSE scalar-float pair packing: `movss` values are interleaved with `unpcklps`, then the low 64-bit pair is transferred with `movq` or `movlps`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN

A `GLOBAL_VAR` address and immediate fields are saved in stack slots, then a loaded value is compared with an immediate and a conditional branch guards a call using a stack address in `rdi` and constants in `esi` and `edx`.
Repeatedly sign-extend byte values into wider registers with `movsx`, often from `al` or a byte-sized memory operand, then use the signed result in nearby tests, comparisons, or calls.
Many separate code paths end in unconditional direct jumps (`jmp JUMP_ADDR_n`) that converge on shared continuation blocks, creating a dense, multiway control-flow graph.
The code repeatedly performs variable-count left shifts, using `cl` as the count operand, as in `shl eax, cl`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated `endbr64` landing-pad stubs copy `rax` into a callee-saved register and then jump directly to an internal `JUMP_ADDR`.
Repeated REP-prefixed string operations bulk-initialize memory, with ECX set to a repetition count and RDI directed at the destination buffer.

A recurring pattern is comparing two candidate bounds or pointers with `cmp`, selecting one with a condition-code `cmov`, then testing the selected value and conditionally branching on whether it is zero.
Multiple conditional and unconditional branches converge on shared local basic blocks, with repeated `jz`, `jnz`, or `jmp` instructions naming the same `JUMP_ADDR_n` target.
NO CLEAR PATTERN

REP-prefixed x86 string operations perform counted bulk memory work, with RCX supplying the count and RDI the destination; copy forms use RSI as the source, while fill forms take the repeated value from AL/EAX.

A sign-bit branch implements unsigned 64-bit integer-to-scalar-SSE conversion: high-bit-set values are shifted right, have their low bit restored with `or`, then pass through `cvtsi2sd` or `cvtsi2ss` and are doubled with `addsd` or `addss`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated `bt` instructions test a bit selected by a register or immediate operand, with the carry flag feeding a nearby conditional branch such as `jnb`.
Dense control flow with repeated conditional branches such as `jz`, `jbe`, `jl`, and `jg` targeting local `JUMP_ADDR_n` blocks that funnel into a shared continuation.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
The code tests the low byte in `AL` against an immediate with `test al, CONST`, then branches conditionally with `jz` or `jnz`.

The code repeatedly stages a runtime array or table index in a general-purpose register, then uses it in base-plus-index addressing to access elements, often with a scaled index such as `index*4` or `index*8`.

A helper’s EAX result is treated as a signed status (`test eax,eax; js ...`), then combined with a second integer argument and status-threshold branches to determine the adjusted status returned in EAX.

A long linear sequence of pointer-identity checks loads a pointer from a stack slot, compares it with successive registers, branches on equality, and on the nonmatching path passes a field address formed with `lea rsi,[rax+CONST]` to a call.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated variable-size stack-allocation sequences compute an aligned size, adjust `rsp` in bounded steps, and touch each new stack region with an `or` memory instruction.
Constructing packed 16-bit values by placing separately extracted or computed bytes into legacy high- and low-byte registers such as AL/AH or BL/BH, then using the combined word register.
NO CLEAR PATTERN

The code computes and aligns a runtime-sized stack allocation, adjusts `rsp` in bounded steps, and probes the newly allocated stack with writes such as `or [rsp+rax+CONST+var_xxx], CONST`, using branches to repeat the probes.
Sign-extend sequence lengths, form 8-byte-scaled end pointers with `lea`, compare the endpoints for equality, then advance paired pointers by a fixed stride in a loop until one reaches its endpoint.
Several routines materialize comparison flags with `sbb reg,reg` after `cmp`, then use the resulting all-zero/all-one mask in `and`, `add`, or `sub` expressions.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A loop-carried cursor advances by a fixed stride, is saved back to a stack slot, and is compared with a saved endpoint to control the loop.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A switch-style dispatch compares an integer register or stack value against successive immediate constants with `cmp`/`jz` branches to distinct case targets, typically followed by a default `jmp`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated lock-prefixed atomic read-modify-write instructions appear within conditional-branch sequences.
A dense switch-like dispatch expands into many case-specific branches and short blocks that jump to shared labeled destinations.
The code repeatedly checks a just-returned call result in `eax` or `al` with flag-setting instructions, then immediately branches conditionally on those flags.
Repeated calls pass pointers to global or static data, formed with `lea` and placed in argument registers, often alongside immediate scalar arguments in `esi` or `edx`.
The callee-saved `rbx` register holds a live value across calls and is reused or updated in subsequent memory and address calculations.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated conditional checks of call results, typically `test eax,eax` followed by `jz` or `jnz` to a labeled control-flow path.
A multi-argument SysV x86-64 call setup that pushes extra arguments onto the stack, loads the argument registers, then calls `cs:xxx`.
Repeated call sequences capture a returned pointer in `r13`, pass it in `rdi`, store it to `[rbx+CONST]`, then make further calls using `rbp` and `r13` as arguments.
The code frequently clears the fifth System V argument register with `xor r8d, r8d` as part of call-argument setup.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A SysV x86-64 variadic-function entry sequence spills incoming argument registers to the stack, then uses `test al, al` and a conditional branch to guard `movaps` saves of `xmm0`–`xmm7`.
A recurring lookup idiom doubles an index with `add rax, rax`, adds a base pointer with `add rax, rdx`, then loads a zero-extended byte from the computed address with `movzx`.

A bounds-checked multiway switch dispatches through a relative jump table, loading a sign-extended 32-bit offset with a scaled index, adding the table base, then jumping indirectly through the result.
A 32-bit value is conditionally selected into `r14d` with `cmovz` or `cmovnz`, with nearby `cmp` or `test` instructions setting the condition flags.
The code zeroes stack-local buffers by clearing `xmm0` with `pxor xmm0,xmm0`, storing it with repeated `movaps [rsp+...],xmm0` instructions, then passing the buffer’s address to a helper call.
Counted array loops round the element count down with `shr`/`shl`, process packed chunks in a SIMD load/compute/store loop, then handle the remaining elements with scalar instructions.

Repeated bounds-check branches inside data-structure traversal loops: after computing an offset or difference with `sub`, the code compares it against a limit and branches on the result—often sending `jle` and `js` to the same target.

A repeated pointer-chain traversal loads a next/link field, tests it with `test reg,reg`, and uses `jz`/`jnz` branches to reach null exits and record-processing back-edges.
A recurring pattern is a chain of `cmp` or `test` instructions followed by conditional branches such as `jz`, `jnz`, `ja`, `jbe`, or `jb` that route execution through guard and dispatch blocks.
A recurring scaling idiom doubles a 32- or 64-bit accumulator with `add eax, eax` or `add rax, rax`, then saves or uses the result in subsequent index or address calculations.
A signed integer or address difference is reduced to a scaled index using constant-count shifts—typically `sub` followed by `sar`—then used in indexed address arithmetic.

A computed size is formed with `add`, and unsigned overflow is checked immediately via `jb` or by capturing CF with `setb` and testing it before branching to an error path.
Counted loops over arrays or buffers, where indexed memory operations are followed by a `cmp`/`test` and a `jcc` or `jmp` back to an earlier `JUMP_ADDR` loop body.
Repeated `endbr64` landing-pad stubs move `rax` into a callee-saved register and then unconditionally jump to a local `JUMP_ADDR`.

Long scalar integer-arithmetic sequences repeatedly load byte-sized values from memory with `movsx` or `movzx`, combine them using `imul` and add/subtract operations, and apply constant-count shifts to intermediate results.

The code uses `rep stos` to bulk-fill memory regions, setting up the destination in `rdi`, the repetition count in `rcx`, and the fill value in the accumulator.

The code computes buffer lengths or end pointers with add, subtract, and scaling operations, then uses unsigned branches such as `jb`, `ja`, and `jbe` to guard allocation and memory accesses against overflow and out-of-range sizes.
Repeated conditional checks branch to a shared `JUMP_ADDR` continuation, often with an unconditional `jmp` also targeting that same block.

A recurring pattern is unsigned `div` by a runtime register divisor, often after clearing `edx`, followed by using the remainder in `edx`/`rdx` as a scaled index into a pointer table and accessing the selected entry.
Repeated scalar SSE double-to-single conversions with `cvtsd2ss xmm, xmm/m64`, often followed by storing the single-precision result with `movss`.
The code uses `cmp` or `test` followed by `cmovcc` to branchlessly select between computed integer values, often clamping them to bounds or choosing a minimum or maximum.
Repeated integer and floating-point division, using instructions such as `div`, `divss`, `divps`, and `divsd` to compute quotients or remainders.
